findings.quote: a sustained rise points to leukaemia or lymphoma
findings.explanation: Overstates. A persistently raised lymphocyte count has common non-malignant causes, and this page lists them itself (smoking, an absent or underactive spleen, chronic infections such as tuberculosis and brucellosis). Earlier in the same paragraph the wording is the safer 'raises the question of chronic lymphocytic leukaemia'. 'Points to' reads as a diagnosis and could alarm readers.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with 'a sustained, unexplained rise raises the question of a lymphoproliferative disorder such as chronic lymphocytic leukaemia or lymphoma, and is followed up with a blood film and flow cytometry'.

findings.quote: it flattens the heart's electrical recovery and can cause cardiac arrest
findings.explanation: In hyperkalaemia the ECG shows tall, peaked T waves (faster repolarisation), then loss of P waves, a widened QRS complex and, untreated, a sine-wave pattern, ventricular fibrillation or asystole. Flattened T waves (with U waves) are the hypokalaemia pattern, so 'flattens the heart's electrical recovery' describes the wrong abnormality in a sentence about high potassium.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'it slows electrical conduction in the heart (peaked T waves and a widened QRS complex on the ECG) and can cause cardiac arrest', or simply 'it disturbs the heart's electrical activity and can cause cardiac arrest'.

findings.quote: why B12 status must be known before folic acid is given
findings.explanation: Stated as a universal rule, which collides with the same paragraph's statement that folic acid is advised around conception; that routine supplement is started without a B12 result. The masking problem concerns using folic acid (especially at treatment doses) to treat an anaemia when B12 deficiency is also present. A reader planning a pregnancy could take this as a reason to delay folic acid.
findings.suggestedFix: Narrow it to treatment: 'which is why B12 deficiency is looked for, and treated first or at the same time, when folic acid is used to treat an anaemia'. Keep the conception advice separate, in the NHS wording.

findings.quote: a value below about 30 µg/L confirms depleted stores in an adult
findings.explanation: A fixed diagnostic cut-off in prose, on a page whose rangeNote tells readers to use the laboratory's interval and not a figure from the internet, and contrary to CLINICAL.md (numeric cut-offs belong in a sourced threshold record with a jurisdiction). Cut-offs used by laboratories and guidelines differ, and they differ again in pregnancy, children and inflammation, so 'confirms' is firmer than the evidence.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the figure and soften: 'a low ferritin, judged against the laboratory's decision point, indicates depleted stores'. If a number is wanted, add it as a sourced threshold record with jurisdiction (for example from the NICE CKS page already cited).

findings.quote: the C-polysaccharide of the Streptococcus pneumoniae capsule
findings.explanation: Tillett and Francis (1930) found that CRP precipitated the pneumococcal C-polysaccharide, which is a cell-wall (somatic, phosphocholine-bearing teichoic acid) antigen. The capsule carries different, type-specific capsular polysaccharides.
findings.suggestedFix: Change 'capsule' to 'cell wall'.

findings.quote: The white blood cells of adaptive immunity: B cells that make antibodies, T cells that direct the response and kill infected cells, and natural killer cells.
findings.explanation: Natural killer cells are lymphocytes but belong to innate immunity (innate lymphoid cells); they are not cells of adaptive immunity, so the sentence misfiles them.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: 'The white blood cells that carry adaptive immunity (B cells that make antibodies, T cells that direct the response and kill infected cells), together with natural killer cells, which act in innate immunity.'

findings.quote: amoxicillin
findings.explanation: Amoxicillin is an antibiotic with no role in TSH testing or thyroid treatment, and the page text mentions no antibiotic. It will display as a related medicine next to levothyroxine.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove it from the medications list (the medicines the text names include levothyroxine, amiodarone and lithium).

findings.quote: Thyroid cartilage
findings.explanation: The thyroid cartilage is the large cartilage of the larynx (voice box); it is not part of the thyroid gland, which lies below it in front of the trachea. Tagging TSH with 'larynx' (organs) and 'Thyroid cartilage' (structures) points readers at the wrong anatomy for where TSH acts and which gland it drives. The free-t4 page carries the same pair of tags.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove 'larynx' and 'Thyroid cartilage' from the TSH and free T4 pages unless the anatomy set has a thyroid-gland entry to use instead.

findings.quote: Red cells are normally about 80 to 100 femtolitres in volume.
findings.explanation: A fixed reference interval stated in prose, on a page whose rangeNote says intervals depend on the laboratory, analyser, age, sex and pregnancy and must not be taken from the internet; it also conflicts with CLINICAL.md (no ranges or cut-offs in prose). Intervals differ in newborns and children.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the numbers, for example 'Red cells are fairly uniform in size; the laboratory report shows the interval for its own analyser.'

findings.quote: High-sensitivity troponin is the blood marker that rules a heart attack in or out, read as a change between two samples a few hours apart.
findings.explanation: Stronger than the body of the page. Troponin shows heart-muscle injury, and the page itself says injury is not the same as infarction (pulmonary embolism, sepsis, kidney failure and others raise it). The page also says a single undetectable high-sensitivity result can make infarction very unlikely, so a change between two samples is not the only way it is read.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword to 'the blood marker of heart-muscle injury that, read with the symptoms and ECG, helps rule a heart attack in or out; interpreted against the assay's own limit and, where needed, as a rise or fall between samples'.

findings.quote: to follow flares of rheumatoid arthritis, lupus or vasculitis
findings.explanation: The same page says (lower[1] and the rangeNote) that in lupus the CRP often stays low despite active disease, so a low value does not exclude a flare. Listing lupus beside rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitis as conditions whose flares are followed by CRP contradicts that; lupus activity is usually followed with other tests.
findings.suggestedFix: Drop 'lupus' from the list, or write 'rheumatoid arthritis or vasculitis (in lupus the CRP often stays low)'.

findings.quote: Viral infections including influenza, viral hepatitis and COVID-19; tuberculosis and malaria
findings.explanation: Hepatitis and tuberculosis are listed here as causes of a LOW count and also as causes of a HIGH count (higher[0] 'hepatitis', higher[1] 'tuberculosis'), with nothing to say when each direction applies (stage, severity or pattern). A reader cannot tell which to expect.
findings.suggestedFix: Keep hepatitis and tuberculosis in one list only, or add a sourced qualifier saying when each direction occurs.

findings.quote: a large HDL share is protective
findings.explanation: Causal wording that the HDL page contradicts: that page calls HDL a risk marker rather than a treatment target, says HDL-raising drugs have not reduced heart attacks, and says very high values are of uncertain significance. 'Associated with lower risk' is what the evidence supports; 'protective' implies a causal benefit.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to '(a large HDL share goes with lower risk)'.

findings.quote: Only the fraction not bound to sex hormone-binding globulin and albumin acts on tissues.
findings.explanation: The testosterone page says the free plus albumin-bound ('bioavailable') fraction reaches tissues, because albumin binding of sex steroids is weak. This page excludes the albumin-bound part, so two pages in the same set give different accounts of which fraction is active.
findings.suggestedFix: Align the wording, for example 'Oestradiol that is not tightly bound to sex hormone-binding globulin (the free and loosely albumin-bound fractions) is available to tissues'.

findings.quote: a fever in someone with a count below about 0.5 ×10⁹/L is treated as an emergency (neutropenic sepsis)
findings.explanation: A numeric action threshold in prose. It is close to UK practice (NICE CG151) but neither cited MedlinePlus page states it, and the wording leaves out that neutropenic sepsis can present without fever and that the threshold applies mainly to people having anticancer treatment. CLINICAL.md says thresholds should be separate sourced records with jurisdiction. Separately, the summary overstates the marker ('to recognise a bacterial cause of illness'): neutrophilia has many non-infective causes listed on the same page.
findings.suggestedFix: Soften to 'a fever or other signs of sepsis in someone with a very low neutrophil count, especially during chemotherapy, is treated as an emergency', or add the figure as a sourced UK threshold record (NICE CG151).

findings.quote: once the total rises above roughly 40 to 50 µmol/L
findings.explanation: A fixed visibility cut-off in prose. Visibility depends on skin tone, lighting and the observer (the whites of the eyes show jaundice earlier than skin) and newborn thresholds differ; neither cited MedlinePlus page gives this figure. Conflicts with the page's own rangeNote and CLINICAL.md.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'once the total is clearly above the usual range'.

findings.quote: spontaneous serious bleeding becomes a risk below about 20 ×10⁹/L
findings.explanation: A fixed risk threshold in prose. Quoted thresholds vary by source and context (commonly 10 to 30 ×10⁹/L), bleeding risk depends on the cause and on drugs such as aspirin or anticoagulants, and the cited MedlinePlus pages are not known to state this figure.
findings.suggestedFix: Soften to 'serious spontaneous bleeding becomes a risk only when the count is very low', or add a sourced threshold record.

findings.quote: the one that rises first in fatty liver disease, viral hepatitis and drug-induced injury
findings.explanation: No standard source says ALT rises before AST. In acute injury AST (half-life about 17 hours) often rises and falls faster than ALT (about 47 hours), for example in paracetamol overdose and ischaemic hepatitis. What is true is that ALT is the more liver-specific enzyme and the one most often raised in fatty liver disease.
findings.suggestedFix: Change 'the one that rises first' to 'the one most often raised'.

findings.quote: and in people at higher risk such as those aged 65 and over, people with little sun exposure and people with darker skin
findings.explanation: UK advice (NHS vitamin D page, NICE CKS) is that people in these groups are advised to take a supplement and do not usually need a blood test; testing is mainly for symptoms or signs of deficiency, bone disease or abnormal calcium, phosphate or PTH. As worded, the sentence reads as if these groups are routinely tested, which sits awkwardly with the next clause saying supplements do not depend on a blood test.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the 'people at higher risk' clause, or say these groups are advised to take a supplement without a test.

findings.quote: Kidney failure, some haemoglobin variants (assay-dependent)
findings.explanation: Lists kidney failure only as a cause of a falsely high value. In advanced chronic kidney disease (anaemia, shortened red-cell survival, erythropoietin treatment) HbA1c more often reads falsely low, whereas carbamylated haemoglobin can raise it on some older methods, so the direction is not one-way; '(assay-dependent)' only partly covers this.
findings.suggestedFix: Move kidney failure out of the 'higher' list into the factors list as 'advanced kidney disease can distort HbA1c in either direction'.

notes: All 37 entities read in full (ranges 0:19 and 19:37). No web access used. Nothing rated high: no dose, stop/start-a-medicine advice or promise of safety found, and every unit conversion checks out (g/dL to g/L, glucose 18, total cholesterol 38.7, triglycerides 88.5, creatinine 88.4, bilirubin 17.1, urea to BUN 2.8, free T4 12.9, testosterone about 29, oestradiol about 3.7, 48 mmol/mol = 6.5%, hCG IU/L = mIU/mL). I had about 25 candidates; the 20 above are the ones I would defend, the rest are listed here. (1) Fixed numbers in prose, against the rangeNote and CLINICAL.md (cut-offs belong in sourced threshold records with jurisdiction; the test_reference_range_risk queue lists none of these pages): reported are MCV 80-100 fL, neutrophils 0.5, platelets 20, bilirubin 40-50, ferritin 30; not reported because they are standard definitions that match UK sources: triglycerides 'above about 10 mmol/L' (pancreatitis), eGFR 'below 60 for more than three months' (CKD), AST:ALT 'above 2'. (2) Cross-link tags: ALP is linked to osteoporosis although ALP is typically normal in osteoporosis and the text does not list it; many pages carry arbitrary-looking structure chips (Caudate lobe of liver on glucose, cholesterol, HDL and triglycerides; Circumflex branch of left coronary artery on troponin and LDL; Common hepatic artery and Cystic duct on ALP; Urinary bladder and Rectum on hCG) that read as anatomical claims; 'oxygen-transport' physiology is attached to white-cell, neutrophil, lymphocyte and HbA1c pages. (3) Look-alikes: free-t4 uses 'T4' and 'thyroxine' as aliases and url aliases t4/thyroxine, so total T4 and T3 searches land on the free-T4 page and no page explains total versus free T4 or T3 (acceptable for UK labs, which measure free T4); INR sits in the 'Blood cells' category although it is a coagulation test; 25-OH vitamin D sits in 'Other hormones'; free-t4 says free T4 is 'not distorted by pregnancy' yet its factors list says pregnancy needs trimester-specific ranges. (4) Below the reporting line: neutrophils summary 'to recognise a bacterial cause of illness' overstates; HDL 'a steady fall in heart disease as HDL rises' is overstated at very high HDL, and 'moderate alcohol' appears as an HDL raiser without the UK caveat that no level of drinking is risk-free; INR text lists factor IX among factors whose fall raises the INR (the PT/INR reflects II, V, VII and X; IX affects the APTT); AST text says alcohol depletes the B6 'that ALT needs' (B6 is a cofactor for both enzymes, ALT is more sensitive); troponin 'chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance)' is a contested mechanism; sodium 'correction in either direction must be gradual' is absolute although acute symptomatic hyponatraemia needs rapid initial correction; vitamin D prose credits the 'UK Health Security Agency' while the cited reference is a Public Health England news story; eGFR says CKD-EPI 'in current UK and US practice', but UK laboratories use the 2009 form without an ethnicity term rather than the 2021 refit (low confidence). (5) Signposting: troponin has no emergency-care pointer for chest pain (hCG has one; potassium and neutrophils say a result 'is treated as an emergency'). (6) References: titles agree with their URL addresses everywhere I could judge; I could not check live slugs or section names (MedlinePlus BNP slug 'natriuretic-peptide-tests-bnp-nt-probnp' and eGFR slug look unusual; MedlinePlus encyclopedia numbers for folate 000354 and 003686 and B12 003705; NICE section numbers such as NG28 1.6, NG185 1.2, NG238 1.3 and 1.9, NG145 1.3; PMC ids; Lab Tests Online UK slugs). The urea page cites the NHS CKD diagnosis page (eGFR and ACR) for claims about urea, which it cannot support. free-t4 is not listed as clean only because it shares the thyroid cartilage/larynx tags reported under tsh.
